---
title: "02 — Multiplicative Number Theory"
---

## Counting with the wrong index

Suppose you must count the pairs $(x,y)$ with $1 \le x, y \le 10^7$ and
$\gcd(x,y) = 1$. Iterating over pairs is $10^{14}$ operations. Iterating over
*gcd values* is $10^7$. Same problem, different index, seven orders of
magnitude.

That is the whole subject of this chapter. Nothing here is about numbers being
mysterious; everything is about **re-indexing a sum** so the work collapses:

- from integers to their prime powers, because most quantities of interest are
  determined independently at each prime;
- from pairs to their gcd, turning an exact condition into a weighted sum over
  divisors;
- from all $n$ values of $\lfloor n/i \rfloor$ to the $O(\sqrt n)$ distinct
  ones, because the quotient is constant on long stretches.

Learn the three re-indexings and the formulas write themselves. Memorize the
formulas instead and you will be stuck the moment a problem perturbs them.

## Prerequisites and learning objectives

You need [unique factorization and double counting](../00-prerequisite-audit/chapter.qmd)
and [modular fields and valuations](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd).

By the end you should be able to reconstruct an arithmetic function from its
values on prime powers, prove Möbius inversion instead of quoting it, turn a
gcd restriction into a sum over multiples, and decide between sieving a
bounded domain and factoring a handful of large values.

## Definitions and notation

An **arithmetic function** assigns a coefficient to each positive integer —
concretely, an array indexed from $1$. Coefficients live in the integers or in
a stated commutative ring, and no division is assumed unless a unit condition
is stated.

The standard cast: $\mathbf 1(n) = 1$ for all $n$; $\operatorname{id}(n) = n$;
and $\varepsilon(n)$, which is $1$ at $n=1$ and $0$ elsewhere. Be careful to
distinguish the pointwise product $f(n)g(n)$ from Dirichlet convolution $f*g$,
introduced below; they are different operations and contest editorials rarely
say which they mean.

A factorization $n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$ has finitely many nonzero exponents, and
$1$ is the empty product. Zero is outside the domain of every divisor
transform here.

## 1. Getting the prime factorization at all

Everything below assumes you can see a number's prime powers. For values up to
$10^7$ a sieve does it. For isolated 64-bit values it does not, and trial
division by all primes up to $2^{32}$ is far too slow. The standard pair of
tools is Miller–Rabin to decide primality and Pollard–Rho to split composites.

### Miller–Rabin: turning Fermat's test into a real test

Fermat's little theorem says a prime $n$ satisfies $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$. The
converse is false, so a naive Fermat test has false positives. Miller–Rabin
extracts more information from the same exponentiation by looking at the
*square roots* encountered along the way.

Write $n - 1 = d \cdot 2^s$ with $d$ odd, and consider the chain

$$a^d, \; a^{2d}, \; a^{4d}, \; \ldots, \; a^{2^s d} = a^{n-1}.$$

If $n$ is prime, the last value is $1$, and in a *field* the only square roots
of $1$ are $\pm 1$ (because $x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)$ has at most two roots).
So the chain must either start at $1$ or hit $-1$ before it first hits $1$.
A base $a$ whose chain does neither is a **witness**: it proves $n$ composite,
with no probability attached.

A base that passes is only evidence, so several bases are tried. For unsigned
64-bit inputs the set

$$\{2,\ 325,\ 9375,\ 28178,\ 450775,\ 9780504,\ 1795265022\}$$

is known to be sufficient — it has been verified exhaustively over the whole
range, so the test is *deterministic* there, not probabilistic. (The
certificate is catalogued in the [SPRP base
database](https://miller-rabin.appspot.com/).) Handle $n < 4$ and even $n$
first, reduce every base modulo $n$, and skip a base that reduces to zero
rather than treating it as a witness. Cost: $O(\log n)$ modular
multiplications per base.

::: {.callout-note title="Both outcomes on small inputs"}
$n = 21$: $n - 1 = 5 \cdot 4$, so $d = 5$, $s = 2$. With base $2$ the chain is
$2^5 = 11$, then $11^2 = 121 \equiv 16$, then $16^2 = 256 \equiv 4$. It never
starts at $1$ and never hits $20 = -1$, so $2$ witnesses that $21$ is
composite.

$n = 2047 = 23 \cdot 89$ passes base $2$ completely. One base is never enough;
this is the smallest counterexample and the reason for the base list above.
:::

### Pollard–Rho: finding a factor you cannot see

Iterate $f(x) = x^2 + c \bmod n$ from a random start. Modulo the unknown prime
factor $p$, this sequence must cycle after about $\sqrt p$ steps by the
birthday bound — but you cannot observe it modulo $p$, only modulo $n$.

The trick: if two iterates $x, y$ collide modulo $p$, then $p \mid (x - y)$,
so $\gcd(|x-y|, n)$ is a nontrivial divisor of $n$ — computed without ever
knowing $p$. Floyd or Brent cycle detection supplies the candidate pairs, and
batching many differences into a single gcd makes it fast in practice. The
expected time is heuristically $O(\sqrt p)$ for the smallest factor $p$,
usually quoted as $O(n^{1/4})$ for a balanced semiprime.

**Pitfalls.** Handle $n < 2$ separately; use unsigned 128-bit multiplication;
restart with a new $c$ when the gcd comes back as $n$ itself; remember the
recursion receives prime powers as well as semiprimes, so re-test primality at
each level; and accept that the runtime bound is heuristic, not worst-case.

## 2. Multiplicative functions: local data determines global

A function $f$ is **multiplicative** when $f(1) = 1$ and $f(ab) = f(a)f(b)$
for *coprime* $a, b$. Combined with unique factorization, this says something
strong and very usable:

$$f(n) = \prod_p f(p^{e_p}).$$

A multiplicative function is completely specified by its values on prime
powers. That is why sieves that build $f$ one prime at a time are possible at
all, and why "compute $f$ for all $n \le N$" is an $O(N)$ task rather than $N$
independent factorizations.

The coprimality hypothesis is not decoration. $f(ab) = f(a)f(b)$ can fail
badly when $a$ and $b$ share a prime: $\varphi(2)\varphi(2) = 1$ while
$\varphi(4) = 2$. Functions that do satisfy it unconditionally are called
*completely multiplicative*; $\operatorname{id}$ is, $\varphi$ is not.

| $f(n)$ | value at $p^e$ | what it counts |
|---|---:|---|
| $\varphi$ | $p^e - p^{e-1}$ | units modulo $n$ |
| $\mu$ | $-1$ if $e = 1$, else $0$ | the Dirichlet inverse of $\mathbf 1$ |
| $\tau$ | $e + 1$ | divisors of $n$ |
| $\sigma_k$ | $1 + p^k + \cdots + p^{ek}$ | $k$-th powers of the divisors, summed |

Each entry is a small count, and each is worth deriving once.

- **Totient at $p^e$:** among the $p^e$ residues, the non-units are exactly the
  $p^{e-1}$ multiples of $p$. Multiplicativity across different primes is CRT:
  a unit modulo $ab$ is exactly an independent pair of units modulo $a$ and
  modulo $b$.
- **Divisor count and divisor sums:** a divisor picks each exponent
  independently from $0, \ldots, e_p$, which is a product over primes.
- **Möbius:** define $\mu(1) = 1$, $\mu(n) = 0$ if any exponent exceeds one,
  and $\mu(n) = (-1)^r$ for a product of $r$ distinct primes. Multiplicative,
  again by independent choices per prime. Its meaning is inclusion–exclusion
  signs, made explicit in Section 3.

### The linear sieve, and its one clever rule

Building all these up to $N$ in $O(N)$ rests on a single idea: **visit each
composite exactly once, through its least prime factor.** Every composite $x$
has a unique representation $x = i \cdot p$ where $p = \operatorname{lpf}(x)$
and $i = x/p$, and this is the one the sieve emits.

Concretely, loop $i = 2, \ldots, N$, and for each known prime
$p \le \operatorname{lpf}(i)$ with $ip \le N$, emit $ip$. The famous "break
when $p \mid i$" rule is exactly the condition $p \le \operatorname{lpf}(i)$;
without it, composites are emitted several times and the running time
degrades, but worse, the value updates become wrong.

The updates need to know whether $p$ already divides $i$, because that decides
whether the exponent of $p$ is fresh:

- if $p \nmid i$: $\mu(ip) = -\mu(i)$ and $\varphi(ip) = (p-1)\varphi(i)$;
- if $p \mid i$: $\mu(ip) = 0$ and $\varphi(ip) = p\,\varphi(i)$.

Both lines are just the prime-power table applied locally. For a general
multiplicative $f$ you additionally need to store, for each $i$, the exponent
of its least prime (or the value $f$ takes on that prime power), since the
local factor changes from $f(p^e)$ to $f(p^{e+1})$. Total cost: $O(N)$ time
and memory, producing primes, $\mu$, $\varphi$, and any similar function
simultaneously.

## 3. Dirichlet convolution and Möbius inversion

Convolution of arrays combines indices by addition. There is an analogous
operation for arithmetic functions that combines indices by *multiplication*:

$$(f*g)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)\,g(n/d),$$

the sum over all ordered factorizations $n = d \cdot (n/d)$. For example
$(\mathbf 1 * \mathbf 1)(6) = 4 = \tau(6)$, since each of the four divisors of
$6$ chooses one factorization.

Three structural facts, each with a one-line reason:

- **Associative:** both $((f*g)*h)(n)$ and $(f*(g*h))(n)$ expand to
  $\sum_{abc = n} f(a)g(b)h(c)$ — the same ordered triples, grouped
  differently.
- **Commutative:** swap the two factors of each factorization.
- **Multiplicativity is preserved:** for coprime $u, v$, every divisor of $uv$
  splits uniquely into a divisor of $u$ times a divisor of $v$, so the sum
  factors.

The identity element is $\varepsilon$, since $(f * \varepsilon)(n) = f(n)$.

### The key identity, and what it means

$$\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon .$$

*Proof.* For $n$ with $r \ge 1$ distinct prime factors, the divisors with
$\mu \ne 0$ are exactly the products of subsets of those primes, and
$\mu$ contributes $(-1)^{|S|}$:

$$\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = \sum_{S \subseteq [0,r)}(-1)^{|S|}
= \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(1 - 1) = 0 .$$

For $n = 1$ the empty product gives $1$. So $\mu$ is precisely the sequence of
inclusion–exclusion signs, packaged so that "sum over divisors" can be undone.

**Möbius inversion** is now pure algebra. If $F$ is the divisor-sum of $f$,
then $F = f * \mathbf 1$; convolving both sides with $\mu$ cancels
$\mathbf 1$ and returns $f$:

$$F(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,F(n/d).$$

This is worth re-deriving rather than memorizing, because the same two lines
handle every variant you meet (sums over multiples, sums over subsets, sums
over a general poset).

Some identities that follow, and which you will use constantly:

$$\mathbf 1 * \varphi = \operatorname{id}, \qquad
\mu * \operatorname{id} = \varphi, \qquad
\mathbf 1 * \mathbf 1 = \tau.$$

*Why $\sum_{d \mid n}\varphi(d) = n$:* classify each $a \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ by
$d = n/\gcd(a,n)$. Writing $a = (n/d)b$, the valid $b$ are exactly the
$\varphi(d)$ values in $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ coprime to $d$. Every $a$ lands in
exactly one class, so the classes partition $n$ elements. The second identity
is the first one inverted.

### The gcd filter: the workhorse pattern

Here is the identity that solves the problem this chapter opened with:

$$[\gcd(x,y) = 1] = \sum_{d \mid x,\; d \mid y} \mu(d).$$

*Why:* the right side is $\sum_{d \mid g}\mu(d)$ for $g = \gcd(x,y)$, which is
$1$ when $g = 1$ and $0$ otherwise — exactly $\varepsilon(g)$.

The payoff is that an exact, entangled condition on a pair becomes a weighted
sum of *independent* conditions. Summing over all pairs,

$$\#\{(x,y) : \gcd(x,y) = 1\} = \sum_d \mu(d)\,A_d B_d,$$

where $A_d$ and $B_d$ count multiples of $d$ in each coordinate — quantities
that are usually trivial to compute. More generally, when the condition is
"gcd equals $g$", group the pairs by gcd, write down the resulting divisor
relation, and invert it.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked example: coprime pairs in a $4 \times 4$ box"}
Count $(x,y)$ with $1 \le x,y \le 4$ and $\gcd(x,y) = 1$. For each $d$ there
are $\lfloor 4/d\rfloor$ multiples in each coordinate, so

$$\sum_{d=1}^{4}\mu(d)\left\lfloor\frac4d\right\rfloor^2
= 16 - 4 - 1 + 0 = 11.$$

Verify by hand: the rows $x = 1,2,3,4$ contribute $4, 2, 3, 2$, total $11$.

Now a warning about what the number means. For *unordered pairs of distinct*
values, first remove the one coprime diagonal entry $(1,1)$ and then halve:
$(11-1)/2 = 5$. Halving $11$ directly would compound an ordered/unordered
error with a diagonal error — and would not even be an integer.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The dynamic version"}
Maintain $C_d$, the number of currently active values divisible by $d$. Before
inserting $x$, the number of active values coprime to it is

$$\sum_{d \mid x}\mu(d)\,C_d,$$

and only square-free $d$ contribute, so a value with $r$ distinct primes costs
$2^r$ terms. Then increment $C_d$ for those divisors. Deletion is the exact
algebraic inverse: decrement first, then apply the same formula to the
remaining set.

With active values $\{2,3\}$, inserting $6$ gives $2 - 1 - 1 + 0 = 0$ new
coprime pairs; inserting $5$ gives $2$. This is the whole reduction behind the
first contest exercise below.
:::

## 4. Divisor transforms: sieving a whole array at once

When a problem is about *all* $n \le N$ simultaneously, do not process values
individually — transform the entire array.

The **divisor zeta transform** replaces each entry by the sum over its
divisors, $F[j] = \sum_{d \mid j} f[d]$. Looping over divisor–multiple pairs
directly costs $N(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots) = O(N \log N)$, which is often fine.
The faster route mirrors a multidimensional prefix sum, one prime at a time:

> For each prime $p$: for $i$ *increasing* with $ip \le N$, do
> `f[i*p] += f[i]`.

Cost $O(N \log\log N)$. The invariant that makes it correct: after processing
a set of primes, $f[x]$ holds the sum over exactly those divisors of $x$
obtained by lowering the exponents of the processed primes, each counted once.
Ascending $i$ order is what lets a contribution travel up a whole prime-power
chain ($1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8$), and that is exactly why the inverse transform
uses the *same pairs in descending order with subtraction*.

The **multiple zeta transform** reverses the divisibility direction:
$F[d] = \sum_{d \mid j} f[j]$, computed with `f[i] += f[i*p]` for $i$
decreasing, and inverted by subtracting with $i$ increasing.

Which one you need depends on the operation you are trying to diagonalize:
divisor zeta linearizes **LCM convolution**, multiple zeta linearizes **GCD
convolution**. The general poset statement appears in
[Chapter 09](../09-transforms/chapter.qmd).

**"Diagonalizes" means a double count.** If
$h[x] = \sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = x} f[a]g[b]$, then

$$\sum_{d \mid x} h[d]
= \sum_{a \mid x}\sum_{b \mid x} f[a]g[b]
= F[x]\,G[x],$$

where the first equality holds because $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) \mid x$ is
*equivalent* to ($a \mid x$ and $b \mid x$). So: transform, multiply
pointwise, transform back. Flip every divisibility sign and the same proof
gives GCD convolution with the multiple transform.

**Example.** With $f[1] = 2$, $f[2] = 3$, $f[3] = 5$, the transformed value at
$6$ is $f[1] + f[2] + f[3] + f[6]$. This is the integer analogue of the subset
zeta transform, with "submask" replaced by "divisor".

**Recognition.** Reach for these when every operation replaces a value by all
its divisors, when queries involve $\gcd$ or $\operatorname{lcm}$, or when
values are bounded while the number of queries is large.

## 5. Quotient grouping: only $O(\sqrt n)$ distinct floors

Sums like $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lfloor n/i \rfloor$ look like $n$ separate terms,
but the quotient takes only about $2\sqrt n$ distinct values — it changes
rarely for large $i$ and is large-but-few for small $i$.

Precisely: $\lfloor n/i \rfloor = q$ exactly when $n/(q+1) < i \le n/q$, so
once the quotient equals $q$ at position $l$, it stays constant up to

$$r = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{q} \right\rfloor,\qquad q = \left\lfloor\frac nl\right\rfloor.$$

Hence the loop `for (l = 1; l <= n; l = r + 1)` performs $O(\sqrt n)$
iterations, each handling a whole block. Combine it with prefix sums of $\mu$,
$\varphi$, powers, or whatever function the summand carries.

With two numerators in the same summand, compute the block end for each and
take the minimum. Watch the degenerate case: once a quotient reaches zero it
stays zero for the rest of the loop, and evaluating `m/(m/l)` with a zero
quotient divides by zero.

A derivation worth internalizing, because it shows the two pictures are the
same object:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
= \#\{(a,b) : ab \le n\}
= \sum_{k \le n}\tau(k).$$

The middle expression counts lattice points under a hyperbola; the left counts
them column by column, the right by the product.

## 6. Dirichlet inverses and designing a prefix-sum recurrence

If $f(1)$ is invertible in the coefficient ring, $f$ has a Dirichlet inverse
$g$ with $f * g = \varepsilon$. It is computed greedily: the $n=1$ equation
determines $g(1)$, and each larger equation contains exactly one new unknown,
namely the $d = 1$ term $f(1)g(n)$. Solving for it,

$$g(1) = \frac{1}{f(1)}, \qquad
g(n) = -\frac{1}{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d \mid n \\ d > 1}} f(d)\,g(n/d).$$

This is the mechanism behind a family of sublinear prefix-sum algorithms. Here
is the design pattern. You want $G(N) = \sum_{n \le N} g(n)$ for a hard $g$.
Find an easy convolution identity $f * g = h$ with $f$ and $h$ both easy to
sum. Then summing over $n \le N$ and grouping by the $f$-factor,

$$\sum_{n \le N} h(n) = \sum_{d \le N} f(d)\, G\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac Nd \right\rfloor\right).$$

The $d = 1$ term is $f(1)G(N)$ — the unknown you want. Move it to the left,
and evaluate the remaining sum by quotient grouping, which needs $G$ only at
the $O(\sqrt N)$ distinct quotients. Memoize and recurse. That is the Du Jiao
sieve, developed in [Chapter 03](../03-advanced-sieves/chapter.qmd).

## 7. Gaussian integers and sums of two squares

A different flavour of factorization, and a good illustration that
"factorization" is a property of a ring rather than of numbers.

The **Gaussian integers** $\mathbb Z[i]$ are the complex numbers $a + bi$ with
integer coordinates. Their **norm** $N(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$ is a nonnegative
integer and is *multiplicative*: $N(zw) = N(z)N(w)$, because
$N(z) = z\bar z$ and conjugation respects products. Multiplicativity of the
norm is precisely what makes "is $n$ a sum of two squares?" a question about
factorization.

$\mathbb Z[i]$ also supports Euclidean division: to divide $\alpha$ by nonzero
$\beta$, round each coordinate of the complex quotient $\alpha/\beta$ to a
nearest integer. Each coordinate is off by at most $1/2$, so the remainder has
norm at most $N(\beta)/2 < N(\beta)$. With division-with-remainder come Euclid,
Bézout, and — as in [Chapter 00](../00-prerequisite-audit/chapter.qmd) — unique
factorization into irreducibles. The units are the four elements of norm one,
$\pm 1, \pm i$. In code, test the few rounding candidates with exact integer
arithmetic; floating point picks the wrong quotient for large coordinates.

**Fermat's two-square theorem.** A positive integer $n$ is a sum of two
squares exactly when every prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ occurs in $n$ with an
even exponent.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the criterion is true"}
*Necessity.* Suppose $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides $a^2 + b^2$ with
$p \nmid b$. Then $(a/b)^2 = -1$ in $\mathbb F_p$, so $-1$ is a quadratic
residue — but Euler's criterion from
[Chapter 01](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd) gives
$(-1)^{(p-1)/2} = -1$ for $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Contradiction, so $p \mid b$
and then $p \mid a$. Remove $p^2$ and repeat: the exponent of $p$ must be
even.

*Sufficiency.* For $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, cyclicity of $\mathbb F_p^\times$
supplies $t$ with $t^2 \equiv -1$. Put $\delta = \gcd(p, t+i)$ in
$\mathbb Z[i]$. It is not a unit: otherwise Bézout multiplied by $t - i$ would
force $p \mid t - i$, impossible since the imaginary coordinate is $-1$. It is
not an associate of $p$ either, since $p \nmid t+i$. As $\delta \mid p$, its
norm divides $p^2$, and we just excluded norms $1$ and $p^2$; hence
$N(\delta) = p$, i.e. $p$ is a sum of two squares. Together with
$2 = N(1+i)$, even powers of $3 \bmod 4$ primes, and multiplicativity of the
norm, every allowed $n$ is representable.
:::

**Constructing a representation.** For $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, find a square
root of $-1$ modulo $p$ (Tonelli–Shanks) and run Cornacchia's Euclidean
descent to obtain $p = x^2 + y^2$. For $p^e$, raise the *Gaussian integer*:
$(x + yi)^e$, not the coordinates separately. The remaining local cases are
explicit: $2^e = N((1+i)^e)$, and a $3 \bmod 4$ prime with exponent $2e$
contributes $p^{2e} = (p^e)^2 + 0^2$. Combine local pieces with the
Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity, which is nothing but $N(zw) = N(z)N(w)$
written out:

$$(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) = (ac - bd)^2 + (ad + bc)^2 .$$

Normalize signs and ordering only at the very end.

**Worked example.** $65 = 5 \cdot 13$ with $5 = N(2+i)$ and $13 = N(3+2i)$.
Multiply in $\mathbb Z[i]$: $(2+i)(3+2i) = 4 + 7i$, giving $65 = 4^2 + 7^2$.
Multiplying coordinates separately would give $6^2 + 2^2 = 40$, which is not
even the right number — norms multiply, coordinates do not.

This construction produces *a* representation. Counting all representations is
a separate task requiring you to track the choice of conjugate at each prime
and quotient by the unit symmetries.

## Contest checklist

- Multiplicative is not completely multiplicative: $\varphi(p^2) \ne
  \varphi(p)^2$.
- Decide whether your divisor formula uses $f(d)$ or $f(n/d)$ before you code
  it; the two differ whenever $f$ is not symmetric in that swap.
- $\mu(n) = 0$ as soon as a prime square divides $n$; only square-free
  divisors ever contribute.
- Frequency transforms need a bounded value domain. For a few large values,
  factor them and do inclusion–exclusion over their prime subsets instead.
- Quotient blocks must use 64-bit division, and with several floors the block
  end is the minimum over all of them.
- Pollard–Rho returns a multiset of factors with repetitions; compress it
  before enumerating divisors or subsets.

## Ordered practice

### 1. [Mike and Foam](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/547/C) — Codeforces 547C

- **Level:** Advanced · **Language:** English/Russian
- **Trains:** dynamic coprime-pair counting via square-free divisor inclusion–exclusion.
- **Editorial:** [official Round 305 tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/18046)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>On insertion, count active values sharing no prime factor with the new value.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Enumerate subsets of its distinct prime factors and maintain counts divisible by each product.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>The signs are exactly the Möbius values of square-free divisors; make deletion the algebraic inverse of insertion.</details>

### 2. [Steps to One](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1139/D) — Codeforces 1139D

- **Level:** Advanced · **Language:** English/Russian
- **Trains:** expectation grouped by gcd, divisor transforms/Möbius.
- **Editorial:** [official Round 548 tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/66101)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>The current gcd is a sufficient Markov state and can only move to a divisor.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Count numbers whose gcd with a state is exactly each divisor using inversion.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Move the self-loop probability to the left side of the expectation equation.</details>

### 3. [Cubic?](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc238/tasks/abc238_g) — AtCoder ABC238 G

- **Level:** Advanced · **Language:** English/Japanese
- **Trains:** prime-exponent vectors modulo three; offline range-query invariants.
- **Editorial:** [official contest editorial](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc238/editorial)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>A product is a cube iff every prime valuation is $0 \bmod 3$.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Represent the changing exponent vector by a collision-resistant fingerprint or maintain it with Mo's algorithm.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Prefix states are equal exactly when the intervening range has zero exponent vector; account carefully for randomized-hash risk.</details>

### 4. [Alex and a TV Show](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1097/F) — Codeforces 1097F

- **Level:** Mastery · **Language:** English/Russian

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>Store each set through parity of how many elements are multiples of every possible divisor.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Union-like operations become XOR/AND on bitsets in the transformed domain.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Recover membership of $v$ by Möbius inversion; modulo two, only square-free multiples matter.</details>

### 5. [Coprime Arrays](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/915/G) — Codeforces 915G

- **Level:** Mastery · **Language:** English/Russian
- **Trains:** counting by gcd, divisor zeta transform, inversion.
- **Editorial:** [official Educational Round 36 tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/57062)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>First count arrays whose every element is divisible by $d$.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>This counts gcds that are multiples of $d$; invert over the divisibility poset.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>The task needs every upper bound, so take differences of the Möbius formula and accumulate contributions over divisor–multiple pairs.</details>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Editorial guidance: all upper bounds"}
Let $B(i)=\sum_{d\le i}\mu(d)\lfloor i/d\rfloor^n$ and $B(0)=0$, for
the positive array length $n$. The floor changes from $i-1$ to $i$ only
when $d\mid i$, so
$B(i)-B(i-1)=\sum_{d\mid i}\mu(d)((i/d)^n-(i/d-1)^n)$.
Precompute powers, add these differences over all $i=dt\le k$, then prefix
sum. Cost is $O(k\log n+k\log k)$ arithmetic operations and $O(k)$ memory.
For $n=3,k=4$, the counts are $1,7,25,55$. Apply the statement's final
XOR/output aggregation only after reducing each count as specified.
Recomputing a full inversion for every upper bound would be too slow.
:::

- **Level:** Capstone · **Language:** English/Russian

- **Editorial:** [official Round 146 tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/5592)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>Process primes one at a time and fix their exponents in each of the three chosen integers.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>If the exponents are $x,y,z$, this prime contributes the factor $x+y+z+1$ to the divisor count.</details>

## Exercises with solutions

### 1. A multiplicativity trap — concept check

Compute $\tau(12)$, $(\mu * \mathbf 1)(12)$, and $\varphi(12)$ from prime
powers. Then explain why $\tau(12) \ne \tau(6)\tau(2)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* check the coprimality hypothesis before using multiplicativity.

From $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$: $\tau(12) = 3 \cdot 2 = 6$ and
$\varphi(12) = (4-2)(3-1) = 4$. The square-free divisors of $12$ are
$1, 2, 3, 6$ with signs $1, -1, -1, +1$, so $(\mu * \mathbf 1)(12) = 0$, as
$\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon$ predicts.

But $\tau(6)\tau(2) = 4 \cdot 2 = 8 \ne 6$. Multiplicativity applies only to
coprime arguments, and $6$ and $2$ share the prime $2$. Splitting at a shared
prime double-counts that prime's exponent choices.
:::

### 2. Recover an arithmetic function — derivation

Suppose $\sum_{d \mid n} f(d) = n^2$ for every positive $n$. Find $f(p^e)$ and
$f(12)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* at a prime power, subtract consecutive equations.

At $p^e$ the divisors are $1, p, \ldots, p^e$, so subtracting the equation at
$p^{e-1}$ from the one at $p^e$ leaves $f(p^e) = p^{2e} - p^{2e-2}$ for
$e \ge 1$, with $f(1) = 1$.

Möbius inversion says $f = \mu * \operatorname{id}^2$, a convolution of two
multiplicative functions, hence multiplicative. Therefore
$f(12) = f(4)f(3) = (16-4)(9-1) = 96$.

Interpretation: $f(n)$ counts ordered pairs of residues modulo $n$ such that
the pair and $n$ have joint gcd one — the prime-by-prime exclusion of pairs
both divisible by $p$ is exactly the factor $p^{2e} - p^{2e-2}$.
:::

### 3. Equal gcd with a fixed value — modelling

For positive integers $m, k$, count the $1 \le x \le m$ with $\gcd(x,k) = d$,
using only square-free divisors.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* substitute $x = dy$ to turn "gcd equals $d$" into "gcd equals $1$".

If $d \nmid k$ the answer is $0$. Otherwise $x = dy$ with
$y \le \lfloor m/d \rfloor$ and $\gcd(y, k/d) = 1$. Applying the gcd filter,

$$\sum_{e \mid k/d}\mu(e)\left\lfloor \frac{m}{de} \right\rfloor .$$

For $m = 10$, $k = 12$, $d = 2$: $5 - 2 - 1 + 0 = 2$, realized by $x = 2$ and
$x = 10$.

Only square-free $e$ contribute, so after factoring $k/d$ this is
$O(2^{\omega(k/d)})$ terms, where $\omega$ counts distinct primes.
:::

### 4. Regroup a floor sum — synthesis

Derive $\sum_{i=1}^{N} i\lfloor N/i \rfloor = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma_1(n)$, then
give an algorithm using $O(\sqrt N)$ arithmetic operations.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* both sides count weighted lattice points under a hyperbola.

The left side gives weight $i$ to each pair $(i,j)$ with $ij \le N$. Group
those pairs by the product $n = ij$: the weights are the divisors $i$ of $n$,
summing to $\sigma_1(n)$. Hence the two sides agree.

For the algorithm, use quotient grouping: on a block $[l,r]$ where the
quotient is the constant $q$, the contribution is
$q \cdot (l+r)(r-l+1)/2$. That division by $2$ is exact over the integers —
divide the even factor *before* reducing modulo anything, since $2$ need not
be a unit.

Check at $N = 5$: $5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 21$, and
$\sigma_1(1..5) = 1+3+4+7+6 = 21$.
:::

## Summary and reference sheet

- A multiplicative function is determined by its prime-power values; that is
  what makes $O(N)$ sieves and prime-by-prime derivations possible. Shared
  primes break naive splitting.
- Dirichlet convolution sums over factorizations $n = ab$. It is associative,
  commutative, has identity $\varepsilon$, and preserves multiplicativity.
- $\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon$ is inclusion–exclusion over prime subsets;
  Möbius inversion is that identity plus associativity, not a separate fact.
- The gcd filter $[\gcd = 1] = \sum_{d \mid \gcd}\mu(d)$ converts an exact
  entangled condition into independent counts of multiples.
- Divisor zeta ascends prime-power chains, multiple zeta descends; each
  inverse reverses the direction and subtracts. They diagonalize LCM and GCD
  convolution respectively.
- Costs: linear sieve $O(N)$; direct divisor sums $O(N\log N)$; prime-wise
  transforms $O(N \log\log N)$; quotient grouping $O(\sqrt N)$ blocks.
- 64-bit factorization has a *deterministic* primality contract
  (Miller–Rabin with the fixed base set) and a *heuristic* splitting runtime
  (Pollard–Rho).
- $n$ is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ has
  even exponent; build representations by multiplying Gaussian integers, never
  coordinates.
